# How  working  Java program

The Java language is object-oriented, multi-threaded, dynamic and so on,  but  at all  not  these  properties  turn  his  in  most  best  language  for  network  programming.  The main thing here is that Java programs are executed in a virtual machine hosted inside  computer,  on which the program is running.

Java program  not  It has  no  contact  from  real,  physical  computer;  all,  about  what she knows is a virtual machine. This approach leads us to some important  conclusions.

First, as noted above, Java programs do not depend on a computer  platform on which they run. Have you ever developed  applications for several operating systems at once? If yes, then most likely  you did not get pleasure from this process. By the time you're done, you'll probably know  such a mass of details about a particular operating system, which is not even  thought  previously.  When  you  write  And  compile  java program  she  will  work  unchanged on any platform where there is a virtual machine. In other words, Java  program  always  spelled  only  for  the only  platforms  -  virtual  cars.

Second, the virtual machine decides what the Java program is allowed to do and what not to do.  Programs in languages like C or C++ are run directly by the operating system. That's why  they get direct access to the computer's system resources, including RAM and  file system.

Insofar as  Java programs  run  virtual  car,  her  developers  And  decide  what  what you can and cannot allow the program to do. The environment in which Java runs  program is called a runtime environment. Virtual  the machine acts as a bastion on the path between the Java program and the computer on which it  performed. A Java program can never directly access input devices -  output, file system, and even memory. Instead of a Java program, all this is done by a virtual  a car.

When  loading  And  starts  applet,  virtual  a car  fully  forbids  to him  file system access. The virtual machine can only give indirect access to  selected system resources - that's why we trust applets and know they don't  able  destroy  files or  distribute  viruses.

The Java runtime shell architecture allows the program to be pieced together  right in the process of being executed. This is practical because the most important parts of the program  can be permanently stored in memory, and less important ones can be loaded as needed. Java  programs can do this using the mechanism of "dynamic binding" (dynamic  binding). If all your programs are loaded from the hard drive of a fast computer, this  property is not that important. Everything changes as soon as you start downloading a program from  Internet. This is where the limited network connection speed comes into play. In this case Java-  the program is able to first load the part necessary to get started, run, and only  then gradually load the rest. As we will see below, dynamic linking,  except  Total  other things  facilitates  maintenance of Java programs.

The Java Runtime Shell solves several of the main problems encountered in  area of network programming. Since the Internet is based on a colossal  number of different computer platforms, the ability to write truly portable  network programs provides great benefits. Java programs cannot do anything that is not  allowed by the virtual machine. Finally, the runtime shell allows you to create  programs,  able to boot over the network  and launch quickly.

In C and C++, a pointer is an integer representing an address in memory  computer. ## built-in  Job  from  network

From the very beginning, Java was supposed to be a network programming language. We already  familiar with the benefits of using the Java Virtual Machine. She prevents  the possibility of damage to the computer from actions downloaded over the network incorrect  programs,  allows  programs  boot  fast  And  not  depend  from  architecture  computer.

All of these benefits are built into the Java language, and we don't even have to think about them when doing  everyday programming. Since Java was originally designed for the web, in its  application programming interface, API, built-in mechanisms for interacting with the network.  With the help of the API, we can work with the network both at a high level of abstraction, using  URL (Uniform Resource Locator) services, and at the lowest level, simply by moving  packages  data  roundtrip.

We have the ability to write applets that talk to the computer they came from.  loaded. In Chapter 19 , we will write just such an applet. The applet will be loaded with  standard protocol HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol). HTTP is only for  retrieving information rather than exchanging data, so the downloaded applet will  enjoy  own  protocol  for  subsequent  interactions  from  web server.

In this example, we did not encrypt the transmitted data, but if you want, you  you can easily implement it. If suddenly you invent a new mechanism, say, compression  video data, it will be enough for you to write an applet that knows this mechanism, and the server,  knowing how to transfer video. Instead of writing a huge client program and  persuading people to install it, you just write an applet that downloads itself  becomes  client  for  reception  video.  API  gives  to you  way  on one's own  define  methods  and protocols for transmitting data over the network, while independence from the computer  platforms  guarantees that  applet will  work everywhere.

## Java  -  dynamic  language

A compiled C/C++ program is a monolithic file filled with  machine  instructions.  IN  case  big  programs  his  size  calculated  megabytes.

When you write a large project, it often happens that it has already used  written code. This is where libraries come in handy. When compiling, your code is merged with  code from the library, and all this together becomes an executable program. If the library  an error is found, every program compiled with it will need to  recompilation. Java programs do not have this problem. The point is that Java modules  programs are collected only at the moment of its execution, and before that they exist separately from each other  friend.  This  means,  what  modules  Java programs  exist  regardless  from  programs,  which  they  belong.

## Methods

A method in Java is a subroutine similar to functions in C and  Pascal. Each method has a return type and can be called passing  some parameters.

For simplicity, all the methods we will use in our examples will be  announced  static  (static).  Modifier  static,  how  And  other  modifiers  methods,  affects how the given method will behave in an object-oriented program  (more on this below).

First, let's understand the syntax of a method declaration. modifiers, if any.  is, precede the return type specification, followed by the name of the method, and  list of parameters in parentheses. The body of the method that follows is enclosed in a pair of curly  brackets:

<method modifiers>  return_type  method_name  (<options)>  {

method_body

}

The method body can contain variable declarations and statements. Unlike the C language  variable declarations can be placed anywhere in the method body, including after  some  operators.

Below, we'll look at issues related to method return values and how to  passing parameters to methods. At the end of the section, we will get acquainted with a special property of the language  Java, which is called method overloading, thanks to which you can  give the same name to several methods that differ from each other by a list  received parameters.

Returned  values

Each method must have an associated return type. The type is void, which  has been assigned to our main method in the examples in this chapter, is a special way  tell the system that this method does not return any value. Methods whose return value is of any type other than void,  must contain a return statement in their body. The return value may belong to  any of the types we talked about in the "Variables" section - including both primitive  types, and types defined through the class. The following are examples of methods not  returning  no  values,  And  methods,  returning  meaning  certain  type.

### Broadcast  parameters

All variables of primitive types are passed to methods by value. This  means that when the method is called, a copy of the variable passed to the method is made. System.out.println("Current  value  of  i="+i);

}

}

Example  2-13a. Comparison  two  whole  numbers.

public  static  String  compareNums(int  i,  int  j)  {  if  (i==j)  {

# Shell  time  fulfillment  Java

You have a few more chapters to read before you can say you understand  all the subtleties of the Java language. However, understanding the basic structure and basic elements,  that make up a Java program, you should have it by now. Before we move on to  creating our first applet, let's discuss the Java runtime wrapper.  As you probably remember from Chapter 1 , "The World Wide Web and Java", Java Programs  run within the virtual machine. Everything the program has the ability to know about  surrounding  world,  contained  in  shell  time  fulfillment  (runtime  environment),  which  created for this program by a virtual machine. The Java language itself has enough  features that make it every programmer's dream, such as object  orientation, built-in error handling, and the ability to simultaneously execute  fragments of the same program (multithreading). However, the main advantage of this  language, which puts it in a very special position, is its complete independence from  computer  platforms,  which  entirely  ensured  shell  time  execution.

Let's talk about how the runtime shell can change lives  programmers,  passing  on the tongue  Java.

## Processes  compilation  And  fulfillment

Java is a semi-compiled language. As opposed to "just  compiled" languages, the Java compiler does not produce the final compiled file,  ready to run on a computer. Instead, it creates a file that can execute  special system - runtime shell. This means that you can write and  compile a Java program on one platform, then port it to another platform, and  straightaway  same run  without  repeated  compilation.

The .class file generated by the Java compiler consists of so-called  byte codes (bytecodes). Byte codes are nothing more than instructions for  run-time shells, somewhat like machine language instructions, of which  is a compiled C program. The only difference is that if the machine  instructions are executed by the operating system and the computer's processor itself,  byte  codes  entirely  processed  shell  time  execution.  For example,  when

the program requests some amount of memory or wants to access the device  I / O (say, a keyboard or monitor), it will respond to these requests exactly  runtime shell. The program itself never has direct access to  system components. So the Java runtime wrapper securely isolates  Java program from computer hardware. This isolation is of particular importance for  applets - as you understand, users are unlikely to like it if at the same time they  read  web page,  built-in  in  this  page  applet  will do  to  example,  formatting  hard drive.

To some readers, it may seem that Java, due to this, can be considered  an interpreted language, such as, for example, Perl or BASIC. And indeed, .class-  file  exposed  interpretations  exactly  So  same,  how  program  on the  languages  Perl  or  BASIC.

However, Java programs run much faster compared to these languages.  since it is much more convenient for a computer to interpret byte codes than the source code on  Perl languages  or BASIC,  adapted for  reading  man.

In a sense, a .class file can be thought of as a compressed form of a .java file with  original  code  programs,  -  and  compressed  so  the way  what  shell  time  fulfillment  It is not difficult for Java to follow the instructions contained in this file. At the same  time this "compression" is not optimal at all. Any .class file generated by javac or  any other correctly functioning Java compiler always contains more  information than is necessary to carry out the actions programmed in it. This  additional information is introduced into the byte code in order to protect against programs  which  could  would  try to cheat  shell  Java runtime.

What deceit are we talking about here? For example, consider a program that  will attempt to access system components bypassing the runtime shell.  It is impossible to write such a program directly in Java, but some computer  a cracker might try to write something similar directly in byte codes. Here and  the additional information mentioned above, included in the .class files, comes into play:  write manually, without using a Java compiler, such byte code, additional  information that would be authenticated by the runtime shell,  very difficult. As we will see below, this is one of the three main methods that are implemented in  run-time shell to ensure the safety of running applets and reliable  isolation  from  of them components  systems.

Despite the presence of this additional information, programs written in the language  Java are still significantly faster than fully interpreted programs.  languages like Perl or BASIC. On the other hand, in terms of the execution speed of a Java program,  lose out compared to programs in languages that compile directly into machine language  codes (for example, C and C++). Fortunately, there is an original way out of this situation - recently  emerging technology of the so-called "compilation in time" (Just In Time, JIT).  "Compilation on time" means that the byte codes are actually compiled and not  are interpreted into machine instructions when a Java program is executed. At the first  when a program is started, the run-time shell compiles it into machine instructions, and  on subsequent launches, control is immediately taken over by this compiled code. So  Thus, the first time any new Java program is executed on a given computer, it  the speed of work will be lowered due to the time spent on compilation, but on subsequent  runs, this program will run as fast as if it were written in  fully compiled language like C and compiled for a given computer  platforms.

# Identifiers  And  usage  standard  Unicode

Identifiers are names assigned to various program elements. Any  an object created in a Java program - a variable, method or class - has its own name, which  is nothing more than an identifier. Identifiers in the Java language are built from  characters  standard  Unicode.  "What  same  such  Unicode?  -  ask  you.  -  Yet  one  standard,  which the  will I have to teach?" Not at all! It is very likely that after you have mastered the material of this  chapters,  to you  more  never  in  life  not  have to  meet with  standard  Unicode.

The Java developers set themselves the goal of making the language as portable as possible.  is such that it can be used with equal success by programmers working outside  only on different computer platforms, but also living in different countries and speaking  different languages. Support for foreign languages has become relevant in recent years, when  many computer companies moved to conquer markets in other countries and  continents. Nowadays, most computer programs are written with  using English, so programmers in countries where this language is  foreign, forced to actually work in a foreign language. Studying computers and without  This is given to many people with great difficulty. Why complicate life even more? Standard  Unicode was designed specifically to help people in other countries work with  computers.

The Unicode standard was developed by an organization called the Unicode Consortium (Unicode  Consortium), and its first version was published in 1990\. This standard unifies  character encoding of the alphabets of most modern and ancient languages. Each character for  The Unicode standard is encoded with 16 bits. Most users work with symbols,  encoded according to the ASCII standard, according to which each character is encoded 7  bits. Increasing the number of bits per character in the Unicode standard allows for a wider set  encoded characters by adding to it letters of other alphabets and letters with diacritics  icons that are used in many languages. All Java programs are coded with  using Unicode, and all strings and single characters used in programs  stored in memory in  form  16-bit codes.

Means  whether  this,  what  to you  have to  teach  yet  one  encoding  characters?  Certainly,  no.  More

Moreover, the use of Unicode will most likely not affect your practical  job as a programmer. If you do not use any symbols in your programs,  beyond the limits of the Latin alphabet, then you may not think about it at all and  keep writing programs the way you've been doing it all your life. By transforming your  ASCII file to a file encoded according to the Unicode standard, the Java compiler will take care of it, so  initial  program texts  to you  not  have to  store in  some  special  format.

So Sun's decision to use the Unicode standard won't do much.  impact on the lives of practical programmers. It is only necessary to remember that certain types  data now take up more space in memory - namely, all strings and single characters  double in size. Of course, at first glance it may seem  lack of language. However, remember that when developing Java, the main goal was not at all  economical use of memory, and efficient programming for the Internet and the ability to  creating portable programs. The fact that these main tasks have been successfully solved allows  put up with somewhat inefficient memory usage for character values. Quite  it is possible that when you need to localize your program for use in other  countries, you will thank fate for what Sun programmers accepted in their time  so  visionary  solution.

Integer constants can be specified in the program in one of three ways: in the form  decimal, hexadecimal and octal values. By default all numbers  are interpreted as decimal and are of type int unless you append at the end  numbers  letter  "l", which means "long".

A hexadecimal digit can have a value from 0 to 15, and for values from 0 to 9  conventional  decimal  numbers, and  for  values  from  10 to  15 - first  letters  Latin alphabet from A to F. Numbers in hexadecimal notation are often used to write  big  numbers  or  for  input  values,  for  which  more  naturally  binary  representation.  Since each digit represents not 10, but 16 possible values, a large number in  hexadecimal  records  takes less  places than  in decimal.

Take for example the number 32767 written in decimal digits. This number is  the largest value a short type can take. In hexadecimal notation, it  has the form 0x7FFF. Whenever you need to indicate that a number is written in  hexadecimal system, you must prefix it with a pair of "0x" characters. Register  letters  in hexadecimal  numbers of value  not  It has.

An octal digit takes values from 0 to 7\. The number in octal notation must  begin with a zero followed by one or more octal digits. For example,  the decimal number 32767 looks like 077777 in octal notation. In other words, if the number  starts from zero, this serves as a signal to the compiler that the digits of this number should  be interpreted as  octal.

Everything  integer  values  possess  property  return  to  beginning  range  (wrapping).

This means that if you try to increase or decrease an integer that is already on  the very border of the range of possible values, this number will jump to the opposite end  its range. For example, let's take a byte variable with the value 127\. If  add one to this variable, its value becomes -128\. There is no mistake here -  integer variables in such situations always change their value from the largest  positive to the smallest negative value. And vice versa: if we subtract 1 from -128, we  we get 127\. The moral is simple: in order not to encounter such a nuisance, you must  estimate in advance what range of integer values you will need and choose for your  variables  corresponding type.

## Numbers  from  floating  dot

The Java language supports regular and double floating point numbers in  according to the IEEE Standard for Binary Floating Point Arithmetic (IEEE Standard for  Binary Floating-Point Arithmetic). The corresponding types are called float and double. float type  presents  yourself  32-bit  number  from  floating  dot  ordinary  bit depth,  but  type  double  -

64-bit  number  from  floating  dot  double  bit depth.

Because all of these flags are defined in the Java language, you can include in your code  relevant checks. Typically, these special conditions are the result of  erroneous actions; for example, if 0 is divided by 0, the result is NaN, and you can  program to find out explicitly. Thus, language support for these special  states  greatly facilitates  Search  errors.

All character floating-point constants are assumed to be of type  double unless otherwise noted. To specify a 16-bit float,  you must append the letter "f" to the end of its numerical notation. After that the compiler will  consider this constant to be of type float. Because Java requires exact matching  types, you will definitely need to use this trick to initialize  variable  float type.

For example,  next  line  code  will lead  to  mistake  at  compilation  due to  inconsistencies  types:

float  num =  1.0;

All floating-point constants are of type double by default,  so to explicitly indicate that a given constant is of type float, assign to  digital  write this number letter  f:

float  num =  1.0f;

# transformation  primitive  types  data

The conversion between two primitive data types is very common in practice.  often. The main thing in this case, as elsewhere, is to correctly imagine that in reality  happening.  inattention  maybe  lead  to  loss  information  or  to  receiving  infidels  results.

Language  Java  requires  compulsory  compliance  types.  This  means,  what  compiler  not  will  automatically convert data from one type to another. You should  convert types explicitly using the type casting mechanism (type cast),  which allows you to tell the compiler what type to convert certain  data.

In Java, type casting is done in the same way as in C/C++. To do this, it is enough to specify  the identifier of the desired type in parentheses before the expression being cast. If  the requested type conversion is possible, it will be performed and you will get the value  desired type. Let's say we have two variables shortVar and intVar, the first of which is  is of type short and the other is of type int. Between these types there are two possible  transformations:

short shortVar = 0;  int intVar = 0;  intVar  =  shortVar;

shortVar  =  intVar;  //  incompatible  types  in  operator  assignments

When compiling this code, assigning the value of intVar to shortVar will result in  issuing an error message. The thing is that you are trying to assign a value with  a larger range variable with a smaller range. This type of transformation is called  narrowing (narrowing conversion), since this reduces the number of bits allocated for  data storage. It is clear that with a narrowing transformation, you can lose part  information,  contained  in  number,  -  or  changing  his  meaning,  or  (in  case  numbers  from

floating  point)  reducing  bit depth  And  topics  most  accuracy  representation.

The Java language forces you to sign that you are aware of what happens when  such a conversion: for any narrowing conversions, you must resort to an explicit  type casting. This is another example of how Java is trying almost violently  methods to introduce a good programming style. Every time you convert to  for example, from a long value (64 bits) to an int value (32 bits), you must provide  what exactly the program will have to do if information is lost. If you  are absolutely sure that the value of the cast integer type long will always fall into  range of type int, then feel free to resort to type casting; otherwise you will need to  provide for some additional actions (for example, issuing a warning  user about possible  loss  data).

So,  to  force  compile  reduced  above  fragment,  necessary  add  in  him  explicit  type casting.  That's how  it will look like:

short shortVar = 0;  int intVar = 0;  intVar  =  shortVar;

shortVar  =  (short) intVar;

Now nothing prevents the computer from making the required assignment. intVar value  will be converted to the short type, as a result of which the high bits of the number will be  discarded, but the sign of the number is preserved. In our case, this will result in 32-  bit  integer  will turn into 16-bit.

## Region  actions

Any declaration of a variable has its own scope, the boundaries of which depend on  where the advertisement is located. Whenever you put a piece of code in  pair of curly braces { }, you introduce a new level of grouping. The boundaries of this  new level determine where the variables created in it will be available, and where  possible to destroy them. The variable is only available if it is defined on  current  level  grouping  or  on the  one of  higher levels.

When the current level ends, all variables declared in it become  inaccessible. However, this does not mean that they are necessarily destroyed, since the rules  variable destructions are more complicated and take into account additional circumstances. At  announcement  variable,  how  you  already  you know  for  her  stands out  plot  memory.  When  current  the block in which this variable was declared ends, it becomes available to  destruction  And  now the solution  about  its destruction will  accept collector  garbage.

Destruction will occur at the moment when no one else will be on this variable  refer. This means that primitive data types are always destroyed as soon as  only  ends  corresponding  block.  Against,  destruction  variables  reference  types

maybe  to be  postponed.

Grouping levels and declaration scopes are most easily thought of as  tree, where each block corresponds to one of the branches. The more nested in each other  grouping levels, the higher this imaginary tree will be. Let's take for  example  fragment  programs  And  let's draw  corresponding  to him  wood  levels  grouping:

int  cnt;

public  void  test1  {

}

}

}

}

# Signs  operations

The Java language supports a large number of operator characters. Operation sign  represents a special character and is intended to perform some action on  one, two or more variables. The most common operation symbols are  plus  (+), minus (-), and equal sign (=).

Operation signs are subdivided according to the number of their arguments (operands). Some  operation signs, such as minus, have different meanings depending on whether they refer to  one or two  operands.

An expression is a construction constructed from the signs of operations and their  operands. Expression evaluation is determined by a set of precedence rules. When they say that  one operation takes precedence over another, which means that it will be executed in the expression  before. An example that should have been known to you since elementary school is the difference between  addition and multiplication. Since in the expression x=2+4*3 the multiplication is performed before  addition,  value x  will be 14,  not 18.

In complex expressions, to ensure the correct order of evaluation of operations, it is better  use  parentheses.  This  not  only  guarantees  to you  required  order  computing,  but  And  will do  expressions  more  readable.  Complete  summary  rules  priority  given  in  tab.  4-5.

## Constructors

A constructor in Java is a special method that is called to create a new  object instance. The constructor of a class must have the same name as the class itself, and not  should return no value. A class can have multiple constructors, but all of them  should  vary  between  yourself  on  quantity  And  types  parameters.  Names  parameters  at  this  don't count - in other words, you can't declare two constructors to the same  class that have the same number of parameters of the same types, but differently  named.  Here  several  examples of constructor declarations:

class  foo  {

foo()  {...} //  constructor  without  parameters

foo(int  n)  {...} // constructor with one int parameter  foo(String  s)  {...}               //  constructor  from  one  parameter  type  String

}

In this example, declaring two one-parameter constructors is legal because  each of the constructors this parameter has its own type. At the same time, you will not be able to declare  yet  one  constructor  how  foo(int  i),  So  how,  although  name  parameter  And  is different,  type  And  number  parameters match  from  one  from  already declared constructors.

## Destructors

Any class can have one destructor - a method that is called at the moment when  the object becomes available to the garbage collector. ## What  such  applet?

The applet combines the elements of a complex graphics window with ease of use and  networking capabilities. In essence, it is a miniature graphic  user interface, similar to Microsoft Windows or X11, which is guaranteed  developers, will have basically the same functionality regardless of  type  computer, them  manager.

Applets are very useful for writing applications for the Internet because they  can be embedded in HTML documents and executed in Web browsers that allow  using the Java language, such as Netscape Navigator 2.0\. To create your own  applets, you need to extend the Applet class and reference the new class in the Web page. Let's  consider  applet  Hello  world",  like  applet,  which  we  were engaged  in  chapter  2 ,  "Fundamentals  programming in Java.

import  java.applet.*;  import  java.awt.*;

## stages  fulfillment  applet

When a Java compatible Web browser loads the Applet class, it first allocates memory  for applet and global variables. Then the init method is executed. (In general, programmers  use the init method to initialize global variables, get resources from  network and install the user interface.) The browser then calls the start method. If  part of the browser containing the applet is visible (which is usually what happens when the applet is only  starts its work), the paint method is called. If the user leaves the page,  containing the applet, the browser calls the stop method. When the user returns to the page  with an applet, the start method, as well as the paint method, is called again. The following code snippet  illustrates how the applet works when the user leaves the page and then  returns to her.

Example  5-2.  applet,  counting  appeals  to  page.

import  java.applet.*;  import  java.awt.*;

public  class  Count  extends  applet  {  int  InitCount=0;

int  StartCount=0;  int StopCount=0;  int  PaintCount=0;

public  void  init()  {

resize(250.75);

InitCount  =  InitCount  +  one;

}

public  void  start()  {

StartCount  =  StartCount  +  one;

}

public  void  stop()  {

StopCount  =  StopCount  +  one;

}

public void paint(Graphics g) {  PaintCount++;

String Output = new String(  "Inits:  "+InitCount+

"  Starts:  "+StartCount+  "  Stops:  "+StopCount+

"Paints: "+PaintCount);  g.drawString(Output,25,25);

}

}

The output of the applet after the first launch is shown in Fig. 5-3\. The applet was once  initialized, started once, never stopped, and at least once  was  redrawn.

### Class  audioclip

The java.applet.AudioClip class is a high level representation of audio data. In that  The class defines three methods: play, loop and stop. The applet class defines the getAudioClip method,  which, given a URL, returns a sound file. Like the getImage method, the method  getAudioClip is actually executed by the applet context; so, the applet is able to use  any  sound  format,  supported  browser. Class  AudioClip, like Image, can be used as soon as sound is requested, but it can  it will take some time to actually load and play the sound. # Interaction  from  user

To interact with the user in real time and track  changes in the Java runtime shell, applets use the concept of an event.  An event is information generated in response to some user action.  (moving the mouse or pressing a key on the keyboard). Events can also be  generated  in  answer  on the  change  environments  -  to  example,  when  window  applet  obscured  others  window. The runtime shell watches for events that occur and passes  information  about  event  special  method  called  handler  developments  (event  handler).

# Animation  at  help  flows

Think of a runtime shell as an office with a single dispatcher that  manages applet methods in response to various events. Our dispatcher is very methodical; is he  must wait for each task to complete before moving on to the next. Suppose  that we want to give it a method that is so complex or repetitive that it  would prevent the controller from doing anything else. The solution in this case is simple - you need  hire a second dispatcher to work on another task. The new dispatcher is the new  flow.

Threads are different from other classes, because they, having received control and started to act,  executed independently in the environment of the method that launched them. In this respect, they are like  processes in multiprocessor operating systems like UNIX. When called  the usual method, the program waits until it is fully executed. But when called  thread method (usually when the thread is running), the method that called the thread continues to execute  during the execution of the thread method. On fig. Figure 5-6 shows the execution of a single thread.  And  two streams.

![](Images/image09219.gif)

#### Rice.  5.6.

You  you can  use  streams  in  their  programs  on the  Java,  defining  extensions  class  thread. This process is described in detail in Chapter 11 , Multithreading. But now we  Let's explain how to allow an applet to use streams. This technique will be useful if,  for example, an applet displays a moving image, but you want the applet to do and  other  useful  things in  animation playback time.

Interface  runnable

As discussed in Chapter 3 , "Object Orientation in Java", the Java language does not take into account  multiple inheritance. An applet cannot directly extend either the Applet class or  thread class. You can define a method that runs inside a thread with  runnable interface. This interface, like the Thread class, is part of the java.lang package.  Can  select  this way:

class  ThreadedApplet  extends  applet  implements  runnable  {

}

Interface  runnable  informs  compiler  what  this  Class  determine  method,  which the  must  be executed within a thread. The method to be executed is controlled by an instance of the Thread class,  created  directly  in  applet.  We'll see,  how  can  use  this  on the  practice:

class  ThreadedApplet  extends  applet  implements  runnable  {  private  Thread  engine  =  null;

//  our  flow

public  void  init()  {

engine  =  new  thread(this);

//  this  flow  now  governs  our  method

}

public  void  start()  {

englne.start();

//  method  starts  be carried out

}

public  void  stop()  {

if  (engine!=null  &&  engine.isAlive())  {

//  if  necessary,

engine.stop();

//  stop  performance  method

}

}

public  void  run()  {

while  (engine.isAlive())  {

//  the code,  located  here,  performed,  till  applet  not

stop

}

}

}

When  applet  initialized,  is he  creates  new  flow,  attached  to  applet.  At  startup  applet, the work of a thread begins, which cycles through its code in the run method, until  applet  not  stopped.

## Simple  methods  for  work  from  streams

Class  Thread  defines  lots of  methods  for  management  streams.  We  detail  discuss  See them in Chapter 11 , "Multithreading". In table. 5-7 briefly describe the most important methods,  which  need to remember.

table  5-7.  General  methods  class  Thread

#### Method Description

isAlive() Returns  Boolean  variable  indicating  is an  whether  flow  current  or  no.

sleep(long) Requests that the thread sleep for a specified number of milliseconds. This method  will throw an InterruptedException if it receives an interrupt signal from another thread.  (ABOUT  interrupts, see  Chapter 11 , "Multithreading".)

## elimination  flicker

Unless you're running a surprisingly super-fast graphics workstation, then when  startup  this  applet  you  for sure  drew  Attention  on the  several  annoying  flicker,  which is the result of the applet's efforts to redraw the screen faster than is technically possible  maybe. The classic solution to this problem is double buffering. Diagram of this  procedures  shown in fig. 5-8.

![](Images/image09221.gif)

#### Rice.  5.8.

When the runtime shell needs to redraw graphics windows -  e.g. when a window was shaded or when an applet requested that the window be redisplayed  redrawn - the applet's modification method is called and the Graphics object is passed to it  graphic  window.  Applet  maybe  request  redrawing  charts  method  paint.  Method  paint  calls the modify method as soon as possible. If the applet requests another redraw  before the update method is called from the first one, the applet is only modified on the first one.  once.  By  default  methods  modifications  simply  transmit  an object  Graphics  method  paint.

An applet can define a virtual screen to draw on instead of  address  directly  to  graphic  window  shells  time  execution.  drawn  The image of an applet can be transferred to a real window using the getCraphics method. This  the method returns the Graphics object associated with the image. The applet will draw on it with  as fast as he can. The applet modification method will display the image on the object  Graphics instead of allowing the applet to display it directly on the screen. As a result  flicker  should disappear.

There is one significant difference between painting the time shell Graphics object  executing and painting the Graphics object of the virtual image. shell window  runtime is cleared and must be repainted completely at each  modifications. A virtual image will retain what has already been drawn on it if it  not explicitly colored. If you want to use such an image to display a moving  drawing, you must redraw the background around the drawing every time you  modify  his,  otherwise  your  picture,  moving,  leave  behind  yourself  footprints.

Now  we  Can  add  double  buffering  to  our  applet  display  cursor,  using  virtual screen image.

Example  5-6a.  Animated  applet  display  cursor  without  flicker.

anim = new Thread(this);  mouse_x  =  125;

mouse_y  =  125;

CursorImages  =  new  Image[10];  int  i;

String CursorParam;  URL  CursorURL;

for  (i=0;  i<5;  i++)  {

CursorParam  =  getParameter("CURSORFILE"+i);  try  {

CursorURL = new URL(CursorParam);  CursorImages[i]  =  getImage(CursorURL);

}

catch (MalformedURLException e) {  CursorImages[i]  =  createImage(0,0);

}

}

}

public  void  start()  {

anim.start();

}

public  void  stop()  {

if  (anim!=null  &&  anim.isAlive())  {  anim.stop();

}

}

public  synchronized  void  update(Graphics  g)  {  paint(OffscreenGraphics);

//  say  applet  paint over  our  image

g.drawImage(OffscreenImage,0,0,this);

//  paint over  real  graphic  window

}

public void paint(Graphics g) {  int  px,  py;

Image  Cursor  =  CursorImages[CursorIndex];  g.setColor(Color.white);  g.fillRect(0,0,249,249);

// draw over the old image  g.setColor(Color.black);  g.drawRect(0,0,249,249);

//  let's deduce  frame

px = mouse_x - Cursor.getWidth(this)/2;  py  =  mouse_y  -  Cursor.getHeight(this)/2;  g.drawImage(Cursor,px,py,this);

public  boolean  mouseMove(Event  evt,  int  x,  int  y)  {  mouse_x  =  x;

Since the Vector class does not have a predefined size, you may be wondering if  how effective it is. Since it is a dynamic structure, we cannot expect  that it will be efficient as an array - as it grows, it will constantly need everything  more memory. By default, space is reserved for 10 objects. Everytime,  when more space is needed, the internal size of the vector is doubled. It's important to remember that  how can you control the expansion of vectors using the constructors and methods described in  tab. 6-12\. The Vector(size int) constructor simply creates a vector of a certain size. If you  know you'll have at least 100 elements, create a vector of that size. You  you can control the growth of the vector by passing a value to the second constructor so that  use this value as a size increment. The vector will then provide space for this.  numbers  elements  every  once,  when  would need  his  increase,  instead of  ordinary  doubling.

You can control the size of a vector after it has been created using the ensureCapacity methods.  or setsize. The setSize method is dangerous if your vector is larger than the new size you  define because all elements after the specified size will be lost. So it's better  use the ensureCapacity method.

## Hash tables

In the same way that vectors are most suitable for storing an indefinite number  objects, hash tables are created to store an indefinite number of pairs of objects. Hash-  table as shown in fig. 6-10 has two columns. One column contains keys, the other -  elements. Each key is associated with one and only one element. If you try  add a key-element pair to the table when such a key is already in the hash table, an element,  corresponding to it will be replaced. By placing the pairs in a hash table, you can access them  elements using their associated keys. In other words, you can pass in hash  table some object, and if this object is one of the keys, will be returned  the element associated with this key. These basic actions can be performed by methods,  given  in table. 6-13.

class  AgeManager  {

private  Hashtable  H=new  hashtable();

//  other  variables

void  updateAge(String  person,  int  age)  {

// name must not be empty!  Integer  intWrap=new  Integer(age);

H.put((String)person,(Integer)intWrap);  return  intWrap.intValue();

}

int  getAge(String  person)  {

// person must be present in the table!  Integer  intWrap=(Integer)H.get((String)person);

return  intWrap.intValue();

}

The basic methods of the Hashtable class allow you to get the desired numbers from the hash table. When  we will pass a name to the ageManager object, it will return the age. On the other hand, we must  create Integer class objects because hash tables don't know how to deal with  primitive data types. Now that we know how to put in and take out variables  from  hash tables,  can  make our  methods more  sustainable.

return  -2;

if (!H.containsKey(person))  return  -one;

Now  we  should  protect  method  put  from  mistakes  And  give  defiant  program  some  information about what is happening. Since the put method returns an object, we can return  old value. This way we can determine if we are adding a new age-name pair  or  replace age  anyone in  our hash table.

return  intWrap.intValue();}

else {  H.put((String)person,(Integer)intWrap);

}

In this chapter, we begin to study a special component of the language called "Advanced  Windowing Toolkit" ("Toolkit for building a window interface", AWT). We will start with  the main elements of the on-screen user interface (Graphical User Interface, GUI),  defined in the java.awt package. The applets we will write throughout this chapter  will  use  the following  Components  awt:

*   input  from  keyboards,
*   fields  for  textual  input  from  one  or  several  lines,
*   buttons,
*   flags,
*   lists,
*   pop-up  menu,
*   stripes  scroll,
*   static  text  inscriptions.

Java allows you to use these basic user interface elements with much  greater convenience and efficiency than HTML. One of the very important tools  available to a Java programmer is the emulation of user input. All of the above  elements allow you to track the movement of the mouse cursor, which makes them more  interactive. For example, the program may display some explanatory or  the sample text in the edit box as the user swipes over it  mouse cursor. Next chapter , "More about the user interface", developing the material  this chapter is about how to implement more complex interface elements. Then,  when we move on to learning about networking (Part 4, "Java and the Web"), you'll already be  be able to create an efficient and professional-looking interface for their programs and  you can  proceed  to  creation  applets,  implementing  connection  from  remote  network  servers  (in  volume  including  And  HTTP protocol servers).

Throughout this chapter, we will create multiple versions of the same applet,  demonstrating the use of various elements of the screen interface. Our applet  designed to convert money from one currency to another; its main function is  accept a number from the user (a sum of money in some currency), multiply it by  definite  well  (conversion factor)  and return  received  result.

# Applet  recalculation  monetary  amounts

Imagine that we are fulfilling the order of a travel agency that wants to  customers through the World Wide Web could get acquainted with the proposed travel routes and  ticket prices. In order to attract more visitors to their page, the agency wants to  provide a convenient opportunity to convert amounts of money from one currency to another  (for example, for customers from other countries who want to know the prices for services in familiar  monetary units). As a Web server administrator, you are tasked with developing  appropriate mechanism. After thinking about the options, you come to the conclusion that Java-  the applet will make it much more convenient and efficient than an HTML form combined with a CGI-  program. We will consider the process of developing such an applet in this chapter. Along the way you  get to know the content  and class features  A.W.T.

Next  chapter  we  let's start  from  clarification  Togo,  how  implement  in  applet  interception  input  user  from  keyboards,  but  then  consider  overall structure  applet.

# Input  from  keyboards

In Chapter 5 , "The Applet at Work," we looked at the concept of events and their handling in Java.  program. As you remember, events of the same type, such as the passage of the mouse cursor over some  area, may refer to some object, while others carry out  interaction between objects. In addition, events can be used to build  user interface, namely, to intercept user impacts on objects  interface.

On fig. Figure 7-1 shows the simplest prototype of the money conversion applet. In this version  the user simply types a number in the input text box and hits enter to see  recalculation result. We use an event handler to intercept the keypress  keyDown, which checks if the pressed key is equal to the value "\n", which  allows you to filter out pressing Enter and provide a special reaction to this key.  (Detailed  description  classes  TextField  And  text area  you  find  in  next  section.)  original  text  this version  our applet  given  in the example  7-1.

import  java.awt.*;

import  java.applet.applet;

public  class  currencyConverter1  extends  java.applet.applet  {  float  conversion_ratio  =  1.50f;

TextField  field1  =  new  TextField(20);  text area  field2  =  new  TextArea(4,20);

//  elements  screen  interface  for  I/O

// (see next section)  public  void  init()  {

field1.setEditable(true);  field2.setEditable(false);  field1.resize(field1.preferredSize());  field2.resize(field2.preferredSize());  add(field1);

add(field2);

show();

}  //  the end  init

public  void  convert()  {

float  currency1,  currency2;

String  InputString  =  field1.getText();  field1.setText("");

currency1  =  Float.valueOf(InputString).floatValue();  currency2  =  conversion_ratio  *  currency1;

String  OutputString  =

"$"  +  InputString  +  "  =  "  +  "#"  +  Float.toString(currency2)  +  "\n";  field2.appendText(OutputString);

}  //  the end  convert

public  boolean  keyDown(Event  evt,  int  key)

//  handler  developments  pressing  keys

{char  c=(char)key;

//  transform  the code  keys  to  type  char  for  comparisons

if  (c  ==  '\n')

//  if  pressed  key  enter,  launch  convert()

{  convert();  return  true;

}

else  {  return  false;  }

}  //  the end  KeyDown()

}  //  the end  applet  currencyConverter1

In this example, we use the keyDown event handler to catch the event  keystrokes. Below, in the "Checkboxes" section, we will also use the keystroke  Enter to start the recalculation procedure, but then we will use the handleEvent method.  This method is a generic event handler that you can use to  intercept even such events for which the program already has other handlers, and,  thus, select events for which you want to provide a reaction. (In the example,  using flags, you will see how you can use this handler to intercept  pressing the Enter key and clicking the checkbox with the mouse.) Thus, to intercept events  there are several ways, and in many cases they are quite interchangeable both in their  functions and speed. In those applets where you will need to intercept a lot  different events, generic event handlers such as  handleEvent or action. Such handlers allow you to collect all the event handling code in  one place, which is usually advantageous in terms of the readability of the applet text and its speed  work.  Broadcast  management  fragment,  respondent  behind  processing  specific  developments,  more often  Total  carried out  operator  switch.

In addition, with the help of the handleEvent method, you can handle entire sequences  events, as well as take into account the spatial coordinates of events within the applet. We  Let's use this in an example using flags, in which the handler, after intercepting  event, checks the coordinates of the mouse cursor to understand where the click occurred - over  flag  or  somewhere  in  friend  place.  Lots of  others  examples  processing  events  you  find  both in chapter 8 , "More about the user interface", and in other chapters of the book, especially those in  which are being developed  educational applets.

# Switches

In order to attract customers from all over the world, our travel agency must provide  the ability to recalculate monetary amounts at the rates of as many different  currencies. Let's create a couple of radio buttons (checkboxes) so that the user can select,  the amount in which currency to convert to US dollars. Like the governing bodies of the same name,  created with HTML, radio buttons in Java allow the user to select one of  several  opportunities,  clicking  on  relevant  mug.  Every  switch  must  belong to some group, and in each of these groups you can mark only one of  switches.  That's how  a new switch is created:

checkbox  Check1  =  new  Checkbox("UK  Pound");

This line creates a new switch called Check1 labeled "UK Pound",  and its default value is set to false (no radio button selected). To create  switch indicating the group it should belong to and its source  states,  use  the following constructor notation:

checkbox  UKCheck  =  new  Checkbox("UK  Pound",  CurrencyCheckGroup,  false);

This creates a radio button labeled "UK Pound" owned by the group  CurrencyCheckGroup and defaults to false. The group that brings together  switches,  is an  instance  class  checkbox group.  Here  how  created  used  in  previous example  CurrencyCheckGroup:

CheckboxGroup  CurrencyCheckGroup  =  new  checkboxGroup();

Remember  what  besides  creation  switch  you  should  also  explicit  way  add  his  in  your applet. In the example below, this is done using the add method, which  used to add all other components. Let's create another one first.  switch,  fellow:

Now  write  check,  allowing  discover,  which  from  two  switches  -  lb.  sterling  or franc  - selected:

if  UKCheck  ==  CurrencyCheckGroup.getCurrent()

{  System.out.println("UK  Pound  is  checked");  }  else

System.out.println("Franc  is  checked")

# Lists

A list box is a set of elements arranged vertically, one or  several elements from which can be selected (highlighted). In the previous example  the user selected the conversion factor for the desired currency using  switches.  but  if  you  going  service  many  different  currencies,  switches  may not be the most suitable for this purpose. Much easier to assemble  choices in a list. Compared to a radio button group, a list allows  arrange  selection options more convenient  and uniformly.

In the applet example below, the list is used to select the currency in which  the user wants to convert to dollars. The List constructor contained in AWT creates  scrollable list box, for which you can set the number of visible at the same time  elements (that is, its height). For a scrollable list, you can also allow or  forbid  choice  several  elements  simultaneously.  Here  how  maybe  to look like  constructor,  creating  new list:

List  CurrencyList  =  new  List(3,  false);

This expression creates a new list called CurrencyList, the quantity  of simultaneously displayed elements of which is equal to three and in which you can select only  one element at a time. If instead of false there was true, this would mean that in the list it is possible,  on the contrary, select several elements at the same time. Adding an element to a list requires  several  more  quantity  preparatory  operations,  how  addition  switch  or  buttons. The text of the new version of our applet, which uses a list to select one of the currencies,  shown in Example 7-4.

Example  7-4a.  Applet  recalculation  monetary  sums,  using  list.

}  //  the end  init

This code snippet creates a new list that is two elements high, allowing  select only one of the elements. Having created the list, we must fill it with elements. This  is done differently than in the previous example, in which we added radio buttons to a group.  New  element  added  directly  in  instance  class  List  -  then  how  switches  we created individually and only then combined them into groups. Here we have enough  create an instance of the List class once, after which you can add any number to it  elements. We then set the cursor in the list to the first element with the method  select(0).  After  this  the whole list  how  one  whole  added  in  applet  method  add.

Development  interface  programs  -  a task  responsible  And  very  difficult.  Instruments,  included in the Java developer kit and designed to organize the appearance  programs that will help you successfully solve this problem. These tools allow you to freely  place elements on the screen without having to specify their exact coordinates and sizes.  The benefit of this approach is not only that the developer does not need to waste precious time  on counting the number of pixels and similar low-level parameters, but also that  programmed in this way, the interface will look more or less the same on  different platforms. Of course, in the details, the appearance of the program on different platforms will  vary, as these little things are highly dependent on the operating system, and even more - on  her  graphic  shells  (for example,  open win,  Windows 95  or Macintosh).

One of the most valuable JDK tools for creating custom  interface is a set of layout managers designed to  visual organization of interface elements. Accommodation managers are a must  used in any applet; even in the simplest applet, on which we are with you in Chapter 7  got acquainted with the main elements of the interface, used the placement manager  by default.

In this chapter, we will discuss all existing deployment managers, as well as containers for  screen elements, which include panels (panels), dialog boxes (dialogs) and frames  (frames). Here you will also learn how to embed menus in your applet, get a list of available in  system  fonts  And  install  fonts  for  individual  elements  interface.  Examples  in  This chapter also uses the applet for converting money amounts from one currency to another, with  which we worked on in chapter 7 , but here we will add many new features to it and  significantly improve its appearance by using more complex components  interface  And  paying more attention  them  placement and layout.

# Programming  external  kind  applet

Before you start setting the appearance of the applet in the program, it is recommended  sketch its screen interface (or at least imagine such a  sketch mentally). This will make it much easier to write code, and it will also tell you the order,  in which it is most convenient to add components to the code. In addition, such a sketch will allow you  understand which groups of components are best combined using panels - special  containers,  containing  other  Components  interface.

# Containers

To combine related controls, the Java API offers three types  containers: panels, dialog boxes and frames. All containers are heirs  class Component and are used as compound objects into which you can add other  elements  screen  interface.  IN  cases  complex  interface  containers  allow  also  arrange groups of elements in different ways relative to each other. For example, a group of checkboxes  or switches with their associated button can be assembled together and placed  in a certain way relative to another interface element - for example, a field  editing.

## Panels

Panels are the most common container type in Java. So, in the given  above example with a group of checkboxes and a button, it would be most convenient to use exactly  panel. The panel is an object that belongs directly to the Container class. Panel  can  use  how  inside  another  container  (for example,  frame),  So  And  directly  in a web browser window. When your interface consists of a large number of elements, almost  always  it makes sense  unite groups  related  on  meaning  elements  from  help  panels.

A panel can also have its own layout manager, independent of the layout manager.  placement of the container in which this panel is included. Suppose, for example, that we  we use the simple FlowLayout layout manager to create a frame containing  components of various sizes. Now you need to put in this frame a group of  five buttons of the same size. This can be done quickly and conveniently by arranging these buttons in  panel and applying the GridLayout layout manager in it (which is just designed for  layout of elements that have the same size), and then placing the finished panel in  frame.

## Window

Window,  how  And  panels,  present  yourself  general  Class  containers.  But  in  difference  from  panels  a Java window is really a window - an operating system object,  existing  separately  from  window  browser  web  or  viewers  applets.

The Window class is never used directly, and only three of them are used.  subclass - Frame, Dialog and FileDialog. Each of these subclasses contains all the functions  original  class  windows,  adding  to  him  several  specific  properties.  For example,  Class  Frame implements a menu container that allows you to add a menu bar to your created  frames. All windows, as expected, have standard buttons for minimizing, maximizing and  destruction, as well as the control menu (control menu). In addition, all windows have a panel  title,  which you  should  fill in when  creating a window instance.

### Frames

A frame is an object that can exist without any connection to the browser window.  Web. Using the Frame class, you can implement the interface of an independent applet. Right after  creation  frame  presents  yourself  empty  window,  in  which  you  should  on one's own  add components  interface.

Frames can contain any user interface elements. Yes, in  example of the money conversion applet we will be working with in this chapter, all  the user interface is framed. Frames can also be created for individual  interface components (for example, a list of users opened by clicking a button in  Web browser window We will see this use of frames in Chapter 18 ). By creating a frame  you can also provide handlers for the click events of the rollup buttons,  maximizing and destroying the window, automatically added to the title bar of the created  window.  except  Togo,  frames  are  implementation  class  MenuContainer,  allowing  add  in  window  menu bar.  Menu  And  Class  MenuContainer  will  discussed below  in  this  chapter.

### Dialogue  window

Dialogs are used primarily to request information one time from  user  or  for  output  small  servings  information  on the  screen.  Dialogue  window  in  everyone  are similar to frames, but have two important differences: first, they are not an implementation  class MenuContainer, and, secondly, they can have a modality - this means that you can  construct a dialog box that will prevent the user from accessing other windows  (including the Web browser window) until the user performs the required  actions  in that  dialog box (eg.  not  press  button).

While creating  dialogue  window  his  modality  given  indicating  special  parameter  constructor call. So the dialog box gives you the choice of whether to allow  user  proceed  work,  not  reversing  attention  on the  dialog  window,  or  same  demand  from  his special  reactions  to a message in  this window.

Dialogue  window  comfortable  for  invitations  user  to  implementation  some  actions  And  to confirm that the user has read the message of the program. Dialogue  windows, unlike frames, do not automatically implement a menu bar. Because dialogue  windows are usually smaller than frames, they are convenient for quick dialogue with  user.

When working with dialog boxes, it is important to remember one rule: each dialog box  must have a frame as a parent. This means that the dialog box cannot be  open directly from the main applet window or from a Web browser window. To create  dialog box, you must first create a frame, even if its only purpose is  will serve as the parent for the dialog box. Only if your applet is already using  frames, you can do without this preparatory stage. An example of creating an empty  the frame that plays the role of the parent of the dialog box, you will find in the section "Dialog applet:  BorderLayout"  in this chapter.

### File  dialogues

The file dialog cannot be used in applets because it is intended only for  programs,  working  directly  in  program  viewing  applets  or  in  interpreter  command line "java". This object is used to pass file descriptors for  loading or saving via the stream class. For more information about file dialogs, see  chapter  12 , "Programming  behind  applet model framework".

# Managers  accommodation

Managers  accommodation  -  indispensable  tool  in  all  cases,  when  number  components  There are more than three interfaces used in the applet. With the help of these managers, you can easily and  quickly provide the desired location of the screen elements relative to each other and  the container that contains them. This mechanism makes it easy to solve problems such as,  for example, dynamically changing the location of components depending on the changing  window size. Setting absolute coordinates for each component cannot be called  a good solution for several reasons: firstly, it is extremely time consuming, and secondly  secondly, changing the position of one component will require recalculating the coordinates of all  the rest. The JDK includes several out-of-the-box deployment managers that are suitable for  for  building  interfaces  in most  applets.

At the time of this writing, several  integrated development environments (IDE) designed to  for creating Java programs and, in particular, for more convenient work with the applet interface.  These environments will include visual tools for developing custom  interface, which will take on most of the work of configuring managers  accommodation. In the meantime, this configuration has to be dealt with by the author of any program,  which explicit  way  enjoys  managers  accommodation.

The simplest layout managers are FlowLayout and GridLayout, the more complex ones are  BorderLayout, CardLayout and GridBagLayout. By default, in the applet window and in all created  panels use the FlowLayout manager, while frames and dialogs use the FlowLayout manager.  BorderLayout.

The following is a description of each of these placement managers and an overview of their use in  examples  from  which we  we will work in  second  half  this  chapters.

![](Images/image09253.jpeg).

## FlowLayout

You are already familiar with the results of the activities of the simplest of the placement managers -  FlowLayout. This manager worked as the default manager in the money conversion applet.  sums, which we wrote in the previous chapter . The principle of operation of this manager and in the very  really  simple  and boils down to  next: each  new added  the component is placed  to the current horizontal row, if there is still room in this row, and if not, then the component  moves down and starts the next horizontal row. Thus, each row, except  the last one, contains as many components as will fit in it at the current width  container.  Content  everyone  row  centered,  then  eat  fights back  to the left  And  right  from  edges  container. This algorithm allows you to achieve quite professional looking  results if you first calculate the size of the area allocated for your applet  on an HTML page using the HEIGHT and WIDTH attributes of the <APPLET> tag. For example, if you  know the exact dimensions of the buttons, you can set the width of the applet so that the buttons  arranged vertically one below the other. However, often attempts to achieve beautiful  locations using this manager require too much effort, which, in  do not pay off in the long run, since almost any resizing of the container destroys  carefully structured (for example, a column of buttons in our example could turn into  several  button lines).

## BorderLayout

We will get acquainted with this placement manager in the sample applets given below in  this chapter. This manager requires when adding a new component to specify  optional parameter that can take one of the following values: South  ("South"), North ("North"), West ("West"), East ("East") and Center ("Center"). first four  parameters cause the BorderLayout manager to refer the added components to  relevant  edge  container  -  bottom,  top,  left  or  right.  Parameter  Center  allows you to specify that this component can occupy everything remaining in the container  free place. Thus, elements added with the Center parameter will change  mine  size,  filling  a place,  not  busy  other components.

The BorderLayout manager is the most commonly used because it is quite practical, easy to use.  use and provides a means to place on-screen elements, which are enough  for most cases. BorderLayout is able to take into account the difference in the sizes of individual  components  And  trying  maximum  economically  use  space  container  -  areas  in  browser window, frame  or dialogue  window.

## GridLayout

Manager  GridLayout  especially  useful  for  accommodation  graphic  elements  And  allows  from  Easily achieve even, uniform placement of components. This manager creates  a lattice consisting of squares of the same size, each of which contains  one component. We will use this manager to build a chessboard in  curriculum in chapter 18 . Each chess field on the board created with this  manager, contains a canvas (Canvas), which, in turn, can contain an image  chess piece. When using this manager, new components are added to  direction  left to right and top to bottom.

## CardLayout

This layout manager allows you to change the set of components displayed on the screen,  directly  in  time  work  applet.  Manager  CardLayout  especially  convenient  at  work  from  panels.

The CardLayout manager allows you to dynamically control the display of components,  added to the container. Components must be associated with special  methods defined in the class - the next, previous and show methods. programmer, so  the way  maybe  start  any  number  components,  but  then,  causing  these  methods,  output  them on the screen sequentially one after another or in random order. In section  "Dynamic  change  components:  CardLayout"  in  this  chapter  we  we will  use  manager

CardLayout to switch between two panels containing our applet's components  recalculation  monetary  amounts.  IN  one  from  panels  will  situated  field,  displaying  current  conversion factor, and a scroll bar that allows you to change this value, and in another  panels - fields for input and output of monetary amounts. These panels will be displayed  simultaneously,  but  in turn.

## GridBagLayout

The most complex layout manager is the GridBagLayout. It uses  the most advanced algorithm for responding to container resizing, and it  allows you to implement a complex interface in which the container contains many components  various  sizes,  some  from  which  should  be  in  one  And  volume  same  exactly  given  position relative to others. When you use this manager, you must specify  location parameters for each component using the setConstraints method. Convenient  just create an instance of the gridBagConstraints class for each component, which will allow  change the location of this component independently of the others. Instances of gridBagConstraints  will be used by the container for which the layout manager GridBagLayout is set,  although in the applet example later in this chapter (see "Exact Placement: GridBagLayout" section), we  we will use the same instance of gridBagConstraints for different components. Here  what the list of placement restrictions looks like that can be set when using  this  manager:

*   gridx, gridy: allows you to create a cell to place the component, specifying it  coordinates, so that the cell located in the upper left corner of the container will have  coordinates gridx=0, gridy=0\. With the GridBagConstraints.RELATIVE value (which  is an  meaning  on  default)  you  you can  specify  accommodation  new  component  not relative to the upper left corner of the container, but relative to the component that  was  added  to  container  directly  front  data:  back to back  to  him  on right  (for  gridx)  or below (for gridy).
*   gridwidth, gridheight: these options allow you to set the number of cells in a row  (gridwidth) or column (gridheight) in the area reserved for this component.  The default values are 1\. The GridBagContraints.REMAINDER value specifies that  the added component must be the last in a row (for gridwidth) or in a column  (for gridheight). The GridBagContraints.RELATIVE value indicates that this component  must be placed after the last one in its row (for gridwidth) or column (for  gridheight).
*   fill: This value is used when the size of the component is less than  the space allotted for it, and allows you to specify whether the component is scaled, and  if so, how. This parameter can take the value GridBagContraints.NONE (by  default), GridBagContraints.HORIZONTAL (which means "stretch the component along  horizontal  how much  maybe,  but  not  change  his  height"),  GridBagContraints.VERTICAL  ("stretch the component vertically as far as possible, but don't change its width") and  GridBagContraints.BOTH ("stretch the component vertically and horizontally as much  maybe").
*   ipadx, ipady: These options allow you to set the padding, i.e. the amount  added to the minimum component size. This means that the width of the component  cannot be smaller than its minimum natural width plus ipadx*2 pixels  (multiplying by two is caused by padding being added to both sides of the component).  Likewise, the height  component  not  maybe  to be  less,  how  his  minimal  natural height  plus ipad*2  pixels.
*   insets:  this  parameter  indicates  external  indent  for  component,  then  eat  minimum  distance  between  component  And  borders  allotted  for  him  areas.
*   anchor: this option is used when the component is smaller  diverted  for  him  areas,  And  allows  specify  accommodation  component  inside  this  areas.  Allowed  the following  values:

GridBagContraints.CENTER (center, default)  GridBagContraints.NORTH (North)  GridBagContraints.NORTHEAST (northeast)  GridBagContraints.EAST (East)  GridBagContraints.SOUTHEAST (southeast)  GridBagContraints.SOUTH (south)  GridBagContraints.SOUTHWEST (Southwest)  GridBagContraints.WEST (West)  GridBagContraints.NORTHWEST  (northwest)

*   weightx, weighty: these two parameters are used to specify the nature of the distribution  white space and are important for accurately specifying the behavior of a component when changing  container size. If for none of the components in the given row the value of weightx  does not differ from 0 (or for the components in this column - the weighty value), then all  the components of this row (or column) will be located close to each other and  centered inside their container. In other words, the zero value of some  of these parameters causes the layout manager to drive all empty space to  relevant  coordinate  to  edges of the container.

## Exact  location:  GridBagLayout

The GridBagLayout manager is the most complex and efficient of the layout managers. In those  cases where your interface contains many components, over the location of which  want to have more control than other placement managers can provide, you should  use GridBagLayout. Suppose the designer recommends for the recalculation applet  sums of money the following layout: the output fields of the conversion factor and the bar  scrollbars to change it should be located on one horizontal line, below  on  center  -  field  input  initial  values,  but  field  for  output  result  must  occupy  all  the bottom of the applet (Figure 8-8). This arrangement can only be achieved with  GridBagLayout manager. In this case, the location of each component is first superimposed  certain restrictions, and only then this component is added to the applet. Manager  GridBagLayout  has  components on  screen  from  taking into account  these restrictions.

![](Images/image09263.gif)

#### Rice.  8.8.

Example  8-6.  applet,  using  manager  GridBagLayout.

public class LayoutGridBag extends Applet {  float conversion_ratio = 1.5f;  TextField field1 = new TextField(5);  text area  field2  =  new  TextArea(4,20);

TextField  ratioField  =  new  TextField(5);

scroll bar  ratioScrollBar  =  new  scrollbar(  Scrollbar.HORIZONTAL,  150,  25,  fifty,  250  );

GridBagLayout gridbag = new GridBagLayout();  GridBagConstraints  Con  =  new  GridBagConstraints();

public  void  init()  {

setLayout(gridbag);

setFont(new  Font("Helvetica",  Font.PLAIN,  12));  setBackground(color.gray);  ratioField.setEditable(false);  field1.setEditable(true);  field2.setEditable(false);  ratioField.setText("1.50");  field1.resize(field1.preferredSize());  field2.resize(field2.preferredSize());  ratioField.resize(ratioField.preferredSize());

ratioScrollBar.resize(ratioScrollBar.preferredSize());  Con.weightx=1.0;

Con.weighty=1.0;

con.anchor = GridBagConstraints.CENTER;  Con.fill = GridBagConstraints.NONE;  Con.gridwidth=GridBagConstraints.RELATIVE;  gridbag.setConstraints(ratioField, Con);  add(ratioField);

con.gridwidth  =  GridBagConstraints.REMAINDER;

First of all, new instances of the layout manager GridBagLayout and the class  gridBagContraints. GridBag is called as the layout manager, which is  an instance of GridBagLayout. If you do not change the weightx and weighty values included in the class  gridBagContraints (their default values are zero), then all components will gravitate towards  center, whereas in this case we do not need this at all. Parameter default value  fill  equals  both,  what  means  what  Components  will  stretch  on  both  coordinates.  Here,  but,  US  not  necessary,  to  band  scroll,  field  ratioField  And  field  input  stretched out

so the fill parameter is set to NONE for them. On the contrary, the field for the output value  should be stretched as far as possible, so its fill parameter is set to  former  meaning  BOTH.  For  parameter  anchor  used  meaning  center,  thanks to  what  all components are placed in the centers of the areas allocated for them. Because at the moment  addition, the ratioField field must be located after the last element in its row, for  of this component, the gridwidth parameter is set to RELATIVE. For scroll bar  ratioScroolBar, which should be the last in the row, the value of the gridwidth parameter  installed  equal  REMAINDER.

In this example, the same gridBagContraints instance is used multiple times,  therefore, before reuse, even those limiters for which we are satisfied  default value, you must explicitly assign the desired values. Import  images

In Chapter 5 , "The Applet at Work," we talked about how to download images from a network  file server via URL. One of the problems we encountered while downloading  images was that the actual image was not loaded until we  at first  not  displayed  his  from  help  method  drawImage.  This  behavior  It was  especially  significant  when we created the animation using the images loaded via the url. This  the problem is not only important for images downloaded from the web - many images  created using complex mathematical formulas that can be calculated  take a long time. The Java API developers at Sun decided to allow  programmers to start using images in programs before downloading or  the calculation process for the given image will actually be completed. It could be  very  useful because  to you  not  have to  wait  the whole  package from  several  images  front  their withdrawal; you can request their output when they are ready for output, and your program  will  continue  work without waiting.

## Usage  class  MediaTracker

Although it is usually convenient to have images available for use before they are  fully  loaded,  there are  situations  when  desirable  suspend  work  programs,  until the data is complete. As we saw in chapter 5 , animation,  consisting of a series of images will look very abrupt and blurry until  will  available  all  Images.  by the most  the best  in  this  case  It was  would,  probably,  wait

receiving  all  images  And  only  Then  start off  animation.

The MediaTracker class, which is part of the java.awt hierarchy, provides an excellent way to do and  managing this process. The main idea behind MediaTracker is that when an image  created, it is added to the list of objects tracked by MediaTracker. To each intermediary  appointed  some  meaning  priority,  And  programmer  maybe  in  any  time  suspend  operations until all objects with the given priority are ready to be displayed. Class  MediaTracker currently only supports images, but Sun is in the foreseeable future.  plans to expand it to play sound bites in the future and possibly  video clips. The most useful methods offered by the MediaTracker class are listed in  tab.  9-5.
